abstract: ArXiv:2605.15841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wegner's [MATH] gauge model is the earliest formulation of pure lattice gauge theory and predicts the topological nature of the confinement-deconfinement transition. In three dimensions ([MATH]), the equilibrium critical behavior of the model is understood in terms of geometrically defined objects, namely loop excitations and Fortuin-Kasteleyn (FK) clusters. This work investigates the critical quench dynamics of this model from a geometric perspective, following quenches from both a high-temperature percolation phase and the zero-temperature ground state. Using time-dependent finite-size scaling analysis, we find that the critical non-equilibrium relaxation of the percolation order parameter is governed by a dynamical exponent [MATH], consistent with that associated with the energy density, [MATH]. Importantly, the value of [MATH] is robust with respect to the initial quench condition and the choice of geometrical objects. Furthermore, we provide a detailed characterization of the kinetics of different geometrical objects during the evolution from the percolation phase. Notably, we observe that the quench dynamics obeys dynamic scaling in terms of a growing lengthscale, [MATH], despite the absence of a local order parameter.
tldr: This paper studies the critical quench dynamics of Wegner's Z2 gauge model from a geometric perspective, focusing on loop excitations and FK clusters.
motivation: To understand the nonequilibrium critical dynamics of a pure lattice gauge theory using geometric objects, which may reveal universal scaling behavior.
method: Time-dependent finite-size scaling analysis of Monte Carlo simulations for quenches from high-temperature and zero-temperature initial states.
result: The dynamical exponent z is found to be consistent with that of the energy density, robust to initial conditions and choice of geometric objects; dynamic scaling with a growing lengthscale L(t) is observed despite no local order parameter.
conclusion: The work establishes geometric scaling in the quench dynamics of gauge models, suggesting universality and potential connections to other topological systems.

title: Gauge-Engineered Tunable Mode Selection In Non-Hermitian Directed-Graph Networks
authors: Zhang Shuang Wenwen Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian physics enables novel control over open quantum and wave systems, but selectively isolating individual modes without delicate balancing of gain and loss remains challenging. Here we introduce a gauge-engineering method in directed-graph networks that support geometry-protected pure decay modes-eigenstates exhibiting smooth exponential amplitude decay along directed paths. In fully connected configurations, a single dominant mode naturally emerges with a large, tunable energy gap from the rest. By adding synthetic gauge fields via phase-compensated non-reciprocal hopping, we can promote any desired pure decay mode to the dominant position, while preserving its amplitude profile. The approach extends to simultaneous selection of paired modes in half-connected graphs and customizable multi-mode distributions in higher dimensions via orthogonal folding. Our method enables robust, loss/gain-free control over mode profiles, advancing applications in single-mode lasers, sensors, and quantum processing.
tldr: The paper introduces a gauge-engineering method to selectively isolate pure decay modes in non-Hermitian directed-graph networks without requiring balanced gain and loss.
motivation: To overcome the challenge of selectively isolating individual modes in non-Hermitian systems without delicate balancing of gain and loss.
method: The authors use synthetic gauge fields via phase-compensated non-reciprocal hopping in directed-graph networks to promote any desired pure decay mode to a dominant position with a large energy gap.
result: They demonstrate tunable mode selection in fully connected and half-connected graphs, and extend to customizable multi-mode distributions in higher dimensions via orthogonal folding.
conclusion: The method enables robust, loss/gain-free control over mode profiles, with potential applications in single-mode lasers, sensors, and quantum processing.

title: Experimental Subdiffraction Source Discrimination Enabled By Spatial Demultiplexing And Single-photon Detectors
authors: Luigi Santamaria Amato, Danilo Triggiani, Cosmo Lupo
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate a universal, parameter-independent test for asymmetric source discrimination. The test allows us to discriminate faint sources well beyond the diffraction limit by exploiting spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) and single-photon detectors. Our test yields a rate of false negatives well below what can be achieved by diffraction-limited direct imaging. Our tabletop experimental setup is inspired by the problem of exoplanet detection, where one aims at detecting the presence of a faint source in the proximity of a brighter one. We present a complete theory, modelling arbitrary modal crosstalk, and collect data across a range of values for the source separations and intensity ratios. We show that SPADE retains an advantage over direct imaging in the relevant regime of small separations and low intensity ratios. Remarkably, we identify an experimentally accessible crosstalk threshold [MATH] below which the exponential rate of false negatives stays well below that of direct imaging. For example, for crosstalk of [MATH], SPADE needs up to one order of magnitude fewer photons than direct imaging to achieve the same error rate. These results demonstrate that SPADE offers an effective methodology for subdiffraction asymmetric hypothesis testing, under realistic imperfections and crosstalk, paving the way to photon-starved imaging tasks.
tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates subdiffraction source discrimination using spatial mode demultiplexing and single-photon detectors, with applications to exoplanet detection.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in distinguishing faint sources near bright ones, as in exoplanet detection, by exploiting spatial mode demultiplexing.
method: A tabletop experiment using SPADE and single-photon detectors, with a theoretical model accounting for modal crosstalk, tested over various source separations and intensity ratios.
result: SPADE achieves lower false negative rates than direct imaging, requiring up to an order of magnitude fewer photons for the same error rate, even with realistic crosstalk.
conclusion: SPADE provides an effective methodology for subdiffraction asymmetric hypothesis testing under realistic imperfections, with potential for photon-starved imaging tasks.

title: Sampling Pseudospectrum For Data-driven Matrices
authors: Caroline Wormell
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many complex systems can be reduced to their key components through spectrally decomposing matrices that capture their dynamics. These matrices can in turn be constructed from data, often by least-squares fitting: examples of algorithms to do this include Dynamical Mode Decomposition and variants, subspace identification and eigenvalue realisation algorithms. Typical outputs of these algorithms include a range of isolated, peripheral eigenvalues capturing persistent emergent patterns in the system. However, there is no objective way to assess which of these discrete eigenvalues are artefacts of finite data error, and which are reflections of a fully sampled operator. n this paper, we present a sampling pseudospectrum [MATH], that provides probabilistic information on the behaviour of finite-data eigenvalues in the complex plane, and an estimator [MATH], which can be obtained by reprocessing our finite data sample. The estimator, which is computationally efficient to implement, allows us to test statistically for the location of the true eigenvalues. This gives us a rigorous and very general way to assess whether the patterns we extract from finite data are likely to be signal or noise.
tldr: This paper introduces a sampling pseudospectrum method to statistically distinguish true eigenvalues from noise in data-driven matrix decompositions.
motivation: Data-driven algorithms like DMD often produce spurious eigenvalues due to finite data errors, and there is no objective way to assess which eigenvalues are real.
method: The authors define a sampling pseudospectrum that provides probabilistic information on eigenvalue behavior, and propose an estimator that can be computed efficiently from finite data.
result: The estimator allows statistical testing for the location of true eigenvalues, providing a rigorous way to assess whether extracted patterns are signal or noise.
conclusion: This work offers a general and computationally efficient tool for validating spectral decompositions in data-driven models, with potential applications in complex systems analysis.

title: Intrinsic-dimension Empirical Bernstein Inequalities For Bounded Self-adjoint Operators
authors: Aaditya Ramdas Diego Martinez-Taboada
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Operator-valued concentration inequalities are foundational to the analysis of modern high-dimensional statistics and randomized algorithms. However, standard oracle bounds are frequently limited in practice: they require explicit a priori knowledge of the true variance, and often explicitly scale with the ambient dimension, rendering them vacuous for infinite-dimensional or heavily structured operators. Motivated by these challenges, we establish the first empirical Bennett and Bernstein inequalities for sums of independent, bounded, compact self-adjoint operators. Our fully data-driven bounds replace the unknown variance with an empirical estimate and rely strictly on the intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension. This structural shift yields computable, dimension-free guarantees that are strictly sharper for non-isotropic random matrices and seamlessly extend to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. We demonstrate that our empirical bounds achieve asymptotic sharpness with the best known oracle rates. Finally, as an independent byproduct, we derive novel empirical concentration guarantees for the intrinsic dimension itself.
tldr: The paper derives empirical Bernstein inequalities for bounded self-adjoint operators that depend on intrinsic dimension rather than ambient dimension, providing dimension-free concentration bounds.
motivation: Standard operator-valued concentration inequalities require a priori variance knowledge and scale with ambient dimension, making them impractical for infinite-dimensional or structured operators. This work aims to remove these limitations.
method: The authors develop empirical Bennett and Bernstein inequalities for sums of independent, bounded, compact self-adjoint operators, replacing unknown variance with an empirical estimate and using intrinsic dimension instead of ambient dimension.
result: The new bounds are fully data-driven, dimension-free, strictly sharper for non-isotropic random matrices, and extend to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. They achieve asymptotic sharpness matching oracle rates.
conclusion: These empirical inequalities provide practical, computable guarantees for high-dimensional statistics and randomized algorithms, with potential applications in operator learning and kernel methods.

title: Amortized Energy-Based Bayesian Inference
authors: Hojjat Kaveh, Ricardo Baptista, Andrew M. Stuart
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider amortized Bayesian inference for nonlinear inverse problems in settings where only samples from the joint distribution of parameters and observations are available. Classical methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo require solving a new inference problem for each observation, which can be computationally prohibitive when inference must be repeated many times. We propose a transport-based approach that learns an observation-dependent map pushing forward a reference measure to approximate the posterior distribution. The map is trained by minimizing an averaged energy-distance objective between the true posterior and the learned pushforward. This formulation is likelihood-free, requiring only joint samples, and avoids density evaluation, invertibility constraints, and Jacobian determinant computations. For function-space inverse problems with Gaussian priors, we parameterize the transport map as the identity plus a perturbation in the Cameron-Martin space of the prior, preserving absolute continuity with respect to the prior. In infinite-dimensional settings, the map is represented using neural operators. We illustrate the method on a finite-dimensional nonlinear inverse problem and two PDE-constrained inverse problems arising in porous medium flow and seismic inversion. The results show that the learned transport captures posterior structure, including multimodality and dominant modes, while enabling fast posterior sampling for new observations.
tldr: This paper proposes an amortized Bayesian inference method using transport maps for nonlinear inverse problems, with applications in PDE-constrained settings.
motivation: Classical MCMC methods are computationally expensive for repeated inference; the authors aim to develop a likelihood-free, amortized approach that can quickly approximate posteriors for new observations.
method: A transport map is learned from joint samples by minimizing an averaged energy distance between the true posterior and the pushforward of a reference measure. The map is parameterized as identity plus a perturbation in the Cameron-Martin space for Gaussian priors, and neural operators are used in infinite dimensions.
result: The method captures posterior multimodality and dominant modes, enabling fast sampling for new observations in finite-dimensional and PDE-constrained inverse problems.
conclusion: The approach provides a scalable, likelihood-free alternative for amortized Bayesian inference, with potential for further development in more complex inverse problems.

title: Statistical Two-round Search For One Excellent Element
authors: Jong Sung Kim Nagananda K G
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate and study a statistical version of Katona's two-round search problem of finding at least one excellent element in a set. A population of [MATH] elements is considered, where each element is independently excellent with probability [MATH], [MATH]. A subset test is noiseless: it returns positive exactly when the queried subset contains at least one excellent element. The goal is to minimize the expected number of tests subject to finding one excellent element with probability at least [MATH], where [MATH], under the restriction that testing is performed in two rounds. Unlike classical group testing, the objective is not to recover the full set of excellent elements, but only to identify one of them. We first show that success is fundamentally limited by the possibility that no excellent element exists. In the sparse Poisson regime, this imposes the necessary feasibility condition [MATH]. When the target success probability is feasible, we prove that the optimal expected number of tests grows logarithmically with the population size. The upper bound is obtained by combining an initial existence test with a second-round separating design; the lower bound follows from an information-counting argument. Numerical illustrations show the feasibility boundary and the resulting logarithmic scaling.
tldr: This paper studies a statistical two-round search problem to find one excellent element in a set using noiseless subset tests, with applications in group testing.
motivation: To minimize the expected number of tests needed to identify at least one excellent element in a population, under a two-round testing constraint, which is a variant of Katona's problem.
method: The authors formulate a statistical version of the problem, derive necessary feasibility conditions, and provide upper and lower bounds on the expected number of tests using combinatorial designs and information-counting arguments.
result: The optimal expected number of tests scales logarithmically with population size when the target success probability is feasible, and a feasibility condition is identified in the sparse Poisson regime.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical foundations for two-round search strategies, with potential applications in group testing and quality control, but does not directly connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Symplectic Neural Operators For Learning Infinite Dimensional Hamiltonian Systems
authors: Yeang Makara, Yusuke Tanaka, Takashi Matsubara, Takaharu Yaguchi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The modeling and simulation of infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems are central problems in mathematical physics and engineering, however they pose significant computational and structural challenges for standard data-driven architectures. In this work, we introduce the Symplectic Neural Operator, a neural operator architecture designed to preserve the symplectic structure intrinsic to Hamiltonian PDEs. We provide a theoretical characterization of their symplecticity and establish a rigorous long-term stability result based on the combination of symplectic structure preservation and learning accuracy. Numerical experiments on canonical Hamiltonian PDEs corroborate this theoretical result and show that SNOs exhibit improved energy behavior compared with non-structure-preserving neural operators.
tldr: This paper introduces Symplectic Neural Operators for learning infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian systems while preserving symplectic structure.
motivation: Standard neural operators fail to preserve the symplectic structure of Hamiltonian PDEs, leading to poor long-term energy behavior. The authors aim to develop a structure-preserving architecture.
method: The authors propose a neural operator architecture that incorporates symplectic structure preservation, and provide theoretical analysis of symplecticity and long-term stability.
result: Numerical experiments on canonical Hamiltonian PDEs show that Symplectic Neural Operators exhibit improved energy behavior compared to non-structure-preserving neural operators.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the benefits of incorporating physical structure into neural operators for Hamiltonian systems, with implications for long-term stable simulations.

title: Vectorized Generalized Nearest Neighbor Decoding For In-block Memory Channel
authors: Yuhao Liu, Xinwei Li, Shuqin Pang, Hao Wu, Wenyi Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work extends the generalized nearest neighbor decoding (GNND), originally developed as a receiver architecture for memoryless channels, to a vectorized GNND (Vec-GNND) suitable for in-block memory (IBM) channels. Leveraging the generalized mutual information (GMI) as an operational lower bound on the mismatch capacity, an analytical characterization of the optimal Vec-GNND is obtained for general IBM channels with Gaussian codebooks. The formalism further provides closed-form optimality conditions and achievable GMIs for restricted variants of the receiver architecture. Furthermore, we formulate a GMI-based joint design viewpoint for Gaussian codebook covariance and decoding metrics. Since the metric optimization admits a closed-form solution for each fixed covariance, the joint design is reduced to an input-covariance optimization problem; for the diagonal covariance family, we derive first-order self-consistent optimality conditions. Numerical evaluations on block noncoherent additive white Gaussian noise channels and phase noise channels demonstrate consistent performance gains over conventional scaling-based baselines, highlighting the substantial advantages and potential relevance of the proposed Vec-GNND in realistic communication scenarios.
tldr: This paper extends generalized nearest neighbor decoding to vectorized form for in-block memory channels, optimizing decoding metrics via generalized mutual information.
motivation: To improve decoding performance in channels with memory, where conventional nearest neighbor decoding is suboptimal.
method: The authors propose a vectorized GNND (Vec-GNND) architecture, derive optimality conditions using GMI as a lower bound on mismatch capacity, and formulate a joint design of Gaussian codebook covariance and decoding metrics.
result: Closed-form optimality conditions and achievable GMIs are obtained; numerical evaluations on block noncoherent AWGN and phase noise channels show consistent gains over scaling-based baselines.
conclusion: Vec-GNND offers substantial advantages for realistic communication channels with memory, with potential for further optimization of input covariance.

title: Interpreting De Finetti's Theorem In The Category Of Integrable Cones (long Version)
authors: Crubill\'e Rapha\"elle
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a connection between two results in the literature on probabilistic semantics: a formulation of De Finetti's theorem in the language of category theory due to Jacobs and Staton, and the generic construction of the free exponential of Linear Logic by Melli\`es et al, that has been instantiated in the model of probabilistic coherence spaces by Crubill\'e et al. The structural proximity of these two constructions is manifest, but making this connection formal requires technical developments on the relationship between the category of stochastic kernels and the category of integrable cones, two well-known categories in probabilistic semantics. We then use this connection to give a characterization of the total elements of the probabilistic coherence space !Bool.
tldr: The paper connects De Finetti's theorem in category theory with the free exponential of Linear Logic in probabilistic coherence spaces.
motivation: To formalize the structural proximity between two constructions in probabilistic semantics: one from category theory and one from linear logic.
method: Develops technical relationships between the category of stochastic kernels and the category of integrable cones, then uses this to characterize total elements of the probabilistic coherence space !Bool.
result: Establishes a formal connection between Jacobs and Staton's categorical formulation of De Finetti's theorem and Melliès et al.'s construction of the free exponential in probabilistic coherence spaces.
conclusion: Provides a characterization of total elements of !Bool, contributing to probabilistic semantics and linear logic, but with limited direct application to the user's research interests.

title: Rethinking The Security Of Dp-sgd: A Corrected Analysis Of Differentially Private Machine Learning
authors: Wenhao Wang, Shujie Cui, Hui Cui, Xingliang Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) is widely used to protect training data in machine learning. Its privacy guarantee is commonly analyzed through a security game in which an adversary infers whether a target record is included in the training dataset from the mechanism output. The resulting privacy leakage is characterized by a privacy curve, which reports the false negative rate as a function of the false positive rate. We identify a mismatch between this formal analysis and common DP-SGD implementations. Existing analyses often model DP-SGD and its variants as the Subsampled Gaussian Mechanism (SGM), where Gaussian noise is added to the sum of clipped gradients computed from a Poisson-sampled batch. In practice, however, many implementations apply an additional normalization step: the noisy gradient sum is divided either by the expected batch size or by the sampled batch size. These mechanisms are therefore better formalized as the Expected-Averaged SGM (EASGM) or the Batch-Averaged SGM (ASGM), respectively. We re-analyze the privacy guarantees of DP-SGD under the EASGM and ASGM formulations. Our theoretical results show that these guarantees can be weaker than the standard SGM-based guarantee, implying that the true privacy leakage may exceed the reported guarantee in some regimes. We further audit four state-of-the-art DP-SGD implementations, including Meta's Opacus library, and observe empirical leakage beyond the SGM-based guarantees. Finally, we audit Opacus versions v0.9.0 to v1.5.4 and derive a corrected privacy guarantee for the latest implementation.
tldr: This paper identifies a mismatch between the theoretical privacy analysis of DP-SGD and its practical implementations, showing that common normalization steps can lead to weaker privacy guarantees than previously claimed.
motivation: Existing analyses of DP-SGD often model it as the Subsampled Gaussian Mechanism (SGM), but many implementations add an extra normalization step, potentially invalidating the privacy guarantees.
method: The authors formalize two variants of DP-SGD (EASGM and ASGM) that account for normalization, re-derive privacy guarantees, and audit four state-of-the-art implementations including Opacus.
result: Theoretical and empirical results show that the true privacy leakage can exceed the SGM-based guarantees, especially in certain regimes, and a corrected guarantee for the latest Opacus version is provided.
conclusion: Practitioners should be aware that DP-SGD implementations may not provide the privacy guarantees assumed from standard SGM analysis, and corrected analyses are necessary for accurate privacy accounting.

title: Quantum Futures Interactive: A Live Demonstration Of Post-Quantum Blockchain Security, Infrastructure Tradeoffs, And Sustainable Distributed Trust
authors: Dongping Liu, Aoyu Zhang, Luyao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in quantum computing introduce long-term security challenges for widely deployed public-key cryptographic systems used across blockchain platforms and decentralized applications. Although post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards are emerging, understanding quantum risk remains fragmented across research, engineering, governance, and investment communities. This demo presents Quantum Futures Interactive, a live interdisciplinary demonstration platform combining educational visualization, participatory interaction, and cryptographic artifact generation to illustrate the transition from classical to quantum-resilient blockchain systems. Participants engage in a structured interaction flow including quantum threat education, sentiment capture, technology prioritization, infrastructure tradeoff exploration, and generation of post-quantum cryptographic outputs. The system integrates distributed trust concepts, sustainability-aware infrastructure considerations, and responsible innovation within an interactive decision framework. The demonstration supports interdisciplinary dialogue on blockchain resilience while aligning with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
tldr: This paper presents an interactive demonstration platform for educating about post-quantum blockchain security, but does not advance technical research in the user's specific areas.
motivation: To address fragmented understanding of quantum risk across communities and to illustrate the transition to quantum-resilient blockchain systems.
method: Development of an interactive platform combining educational visualization, sentiment capture, technology prioritization, infrastructure tradeoff exploration, and generation of post-quantum cryptographic outputs.
result: The platform enables participants to engage with quantum threat education, explore tradeoffs, and generate post-quantum cryptographic artifacts.
conclusion: The demonstration supports interdisciplinary dialogue on blockchain resilience and aligns with UN SDGs, but is a demo/educational tool rather than a research contribution.

title: How Far Back In Time A Digital Twin Reflects The State Of The Physical Object: Age Of Staleness
authors: Sennur Ulukus Ismail Cosandal
abstract: ArXiv:2605.16176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The groundbreaking metric age of information (AoI) has been introduced to measure information freshness in communication networks. As transformational as it is, AoI metric falls short in some applications, such as remote monitoring, since it is a semantic-agnostic metric which does not consider the dynamics of the random process. There is a need to quantify the performance of a remote estimator via a metric that combines freshness and semantic aspects. To this end, in this paper, we introduce a novel metric coined age of staleness (AoS) that measures when the last time that the current estimation was correct. First, we analyze a simple scenario where an [MATH]-ary symmetric Markov source is observed by a monitor via a constant sampling rate, obtain a closed-form expression for the AoS, and show that it is a monotonically decreasing function of the sampling rate. Next, we consider multiple distinct Markov sources, and formulate an optimization problem, where the remote monitor allocates the total sampling rate to tracking the sources. Although the optimization problem is non-convex, its structure is suitable for obtaining a near-optimal solution using the polyblock algorithm, which leverages the monotonicity of the objective function. While the new AoS metric could be applicable in many scenarios, we believe it is particularly well-suited for a digital twin network (DTN) where multiple physical objects (POs) are monitored with a total sampling rate constraint to maintain a digital representation of them, namely, their digital twin (DT).
tldr: This paper introduces a new metric, age of staleness (AoS), for measuring information freshness in remote monitoring systems, with application to digital twin networks.
motivation: The existing age of information (AoI) metric is semantic-agnostic and does not account for the dynamics of the random process, which is insufficient for applications like remote monitoring and digital twins.
method: The authors analyze a simple scenario with an M-ary symmetric Markov source and constant sampling rate to derive a closed-form expression for AoS. They then formulate an optimization problem for multiple Markov sources with a total sampling rate constraint and solve it using the polyblock algorithm.
result: AoS is a monotonically decreasing function of the sampling rate. The polyblock algorithm provides a near-optimal solution for the non-convex optimization problem.
conclusion: The AoS metric is particularly suited for digital twin networks where multiple physical objects are monitored under a total sampling rate constraint, enabling better resource allocation.

title: Breaking The Finite-Sample Barrier In Entropy Coupling
authors: Jun Chen Shahab Asoodeh
abstract: ArXiv:2605.16229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dependence among marginally constrained observations can break a finite-sample barrier. To formalize this phenomenon, we introduce the [MATH], the minimum conditional entropy [MATH] over all joint distributions with prescribed discrete marginals [MATH] and [MATH]. Unlike classical formulations based on independent observations, our model allows [MATH] to be arbitrarily dependent while keeping each marginal fixed. This enlarged coupling space reveals a sharp dichotomy: independent observations reduce residual uncertainty exponentially, whereas dependent observations can eliminate it exactly after finitely many samples. We characterize this zero-entropy regime through necessary and sufficient conditions and give concrete structural criteria under which it occurs. In particular, under mild support assumptions, zero entropy is achieved with [MATH] observations, where [MATH] is the minimum nonzero mass of [MATH]. We also develop a greedy algorithm with monotone approximation guarantees for computing [MATH]. Finally, we show that the same framework formalizes finite-sample limits in distribution-matching representation learning and randomness extraction, where zero entropy corresponds to exact recovery and exact extraction.
tldr: This paper studies entropy coupling with dependent observations, showing that dependence can eliminate residual uncertainty after finitely many samples, breaking the finite-sample barrier.
motivation: To formalize how dependence among marginally constrained observations can reduce uncertainty faster than independent observations, with applications in representation learning and randomness extraction.
method: Introduces a new entropy coupling formulation allowing arbitrary dependence between observations, characterizes zero-entropy regime via necessary and sufficient conditions, and develops a greedy algorithm with monotone approximation guarantees.
result: Dependent observations can achieve zero conditional entropy after finitely many samples (specifically, after the number of observations equals the minimum nonzero probability mass), whereas independent observations only reduce uncertainty exponentially.
conclusion: The framework provides finite-sample limits for distribution matching and randomness extraction, with potential implications for information theory and machine learning.

title: Control-Plane Openness In Near-Term Quantum Computing: A Survey Of Vendor Stacks And Field Implications
authors: Rylan Malarchick
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public access to pulse-level and control-electronics interfaces in commercial quantum computing has bifurcated. The largest superconducting cloud platforms have closed access at this layer, with IBM removing pulse-level control from all production QPUs in February 2025; mid-tier superconducting vendors and the more open neutral-atom platforms have moved in the opposite direction. We survey thirteen commercial vendors across superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and photonic modalities, grading each on six axes of openness at what we call the control plane: the layer between gate-level circuit specification and physical control electronics. The catalog ships as a separate machine-readable artifact under CC-BY-4.0 (DOI: [URL] The bifurcation is documented row by row, with implications for reproducibility, hardware-aware research, and cross-vendor benchmarking. We do not propose an architecture or a reference implementation; we describe what the field has lost as the access landscape has shifted, and what minimally open access at this layer would have to look like.
tldr: A survey of commercial quantum computing vendors' openness at the control-plane layer, documenting a bifurcation where large superconducting platforms close pulse-level access while mid-tier and neutral-atom vendors open it.
motivation: To document and analyze the shifting landscape of control-plane access in commercial quantum computing, which has implications for reproducibility, hardware-aware research, and cross-vendor benchmarking.
method: Survey of thirteen commercial vendors across superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, and photonic modalities, grading each on six axes of openness at the control plane.
result: The largest superconducting cloud platforms have closed pulse-level control, while mid-tier superconducting and neutral-atom platforms have become more open; the paper provides a row-by-row catalog of this bifurcation.
conclusion: The field has lost open access at the control plane, which hinders reproducibility and hardware-aware research; minimally open access at this layer is needed to preserve these capabilities.

title: Second-order Moment Equivalence Of Twisted Gaussian Schell Model Beams And Orbital Angular Momentum Eigenmodes
authors: T. Ferreira, G. Santos, S. Ayala, Lucas Hutter, E. S. G\'omez, G. Lima, G. Ca\~nas, S. P. Walborn
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the covariance matrix of any cylindrically symmetric coherent orbital angular momentum (OAM) eigenmode with quantum number [MATH] takes a universal form depending only on [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], independently of the radial profile, and that this form is identical to the covariance matrix of a twisted Gaussian Schell-model (TGSM) beam.} More specifically, both matrices share the same pattern of zero and nonzero entries, with the off-diagonal blocks proportional to [MATH] and the TGSM twist parameter [MATH], respectively. This result holds for an arbitrary radial profile and provides direct term-by-term identification of parameters between the two sets of beams. We work out the correspondence in detail for three important families: Laguerre--Gaussian (LG), Bessel--Gaussian, and perfect vortex beams (PVBs), and derive the conditions under which each coherent OAM mode maps onto a physically realizable TGSM beam. {Because the covariance matrix governs second-moment evolution under arbitrary ABCD (symplectic) transformations, any two beams sharing the same covariance matrix are second-order indistinguishable at every propagation plane. In particular, the matched TGSM and coherent OAM beams share identical beam-width evolution, far-field divergence, and [MATH] beam-quality factor.} In particular, the well-developed TGSM propagation toolbox applies directly to the second-order moment evolution of the three coherent families. We further show that within each beam family the covariance matrix uniquely determines the beam parameters, with exact uniqueness established for LG modes. Additional results include cross-family second-moment equivalence conditions and a proof that PVB modes form a complete orthonormal basis in the limit [MATH].
tldr: The paper shows that the covariance matrix of cylindrically symmetric OAM eigenmodes is identical to that of twisted Gaussian Schell-model beams, implying second-order equivalence under propagation.
motivation: To establish a formal equivalence between coherent OAM modes and partially coherent TGSM beams at the second-moment level, enabling use of TGSM propagation tools for OAM beams.
method: Analytical derivation of covariance matrices for general OAM eigenmodes and TGSM beams, with explicit calculations for Laguerre-Gaussian, Bessel-Gaussian, and perfect vortex beams.
result: The covariance matrices share identical zero/nonzero patterns and off-diagonal blocks proportional to OAM quantum number and twist parameter, respectively; conditions for physical realizability are derived.
conclusion: The equivalence allows direct application of TGSM propagation formalism to OAM beams, and within each family the covariance matrix uniquely determines beam parameters.

title: A General Differentiable Ray-Wave Framework For Hybrid Refractive-Diffractive System Modeling And Optimization
authors: Jiazhou Cheng, Margaret Gao, Yixuan Shao, Chenkai Mao, Tom D. Milster, Jonathan A. Fan
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid optical systems combining refractive and diffractive optical responses have the potential to support new types of optical behavior, but they are difficult to model and optimize due to the disparate spatial scales and physics exhibited by ray and wave phenomena. In this work, we present a differentiable ray-wave framework that serves as a general model for hybrid refractive-diffractive optical systems and that operates as a plug-and-play module within standard ray tracing pipelines. Our model uniquely applies to both planar and curvilinear diffractive surfaces and can accommodate arbitrary holographic diffractive profiles with high spatial frequency responses. We analyze ray-wave modeling regimes that optimally account for the spatial frequency properties and spatial curvature of the diffractive surfaces, and we demonstrate the gradient-based end-to-end optimization of hybrid refractive-diffractive systems featuring planar and conformal diffractive surfaces. We anticipate that these modeling capabilities will enable new classes of hybrid optical systems relevant to computational imaging and display applications.
tldr: A differentiable ray-wave framework for modeling and optimizing hybrid refractive-diffractive optical systems.
motivation: Hybrid optical systems combining refractive and diffractive elements are difficult to model due to disparate spatial scales and physics of ray and wave phenomena.
method: The authors develop a differentiable ray-wave model that integrates into standard ray tracing pipelines, handling both planar and curvilinear diffractive surfaces with arbitrary holographic profiles.
result: The framework enables gradient-based end-to-end optimization of hybrid systems, accounting for spatial frequency properties and curvature of diffractive surfaces.
conclusion: This modeling capability could enable new classes of hybrid optical systems for computational imaging and display applications.

title: Parametrically Driven Pure-quartic Solitons
authors: Pengfei Li, Lijing Xing, Dongdong Wang, Dumitru Mihalache, David Laroze, Boris A. Malomed
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametrically driven solitons are self-trapped modes in various physical settings, including optics, magnetics, etc. So far, the analysis was focused on the existence, stability, and dynamics of such solitons in systems including the second-order group-velocity dispersion (GVD), linear loss, parametric gain, and cubic nonlinearity. Here, we report the existence of quiescent parametrically driven pure-quartic solitons (PDPQSs) in the full system, and moving PDPQSs in the absence of losses. A systematic analysis reveals stability domains for the solitons in the system's parameter space. Evolution of unstable states is explored too, and it is demonstrated that collisions between traveling stable PDPQSs are elastic.
tldr: This paper studies parametrically driven pure-quartic solitons in nonlinear optical systems, focusing on their existence, stability, and collisions.
motivation: To extend the study of parametrically driven solitons from systems with second-order dispersion to those with pure fourth-order dispersion, which is relevant to advanced optical fiber communications and mode-locked lasers.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis and numerical simulations based on the parametrically driven nonlinear Schrödinger equation with fourth-order dispersion, linear loss, parametric gain, and cubic nonlinearity.
result: They find stable quiescent and moving pure-quartic solitons, map stability domains in parameter space, and show that collisions between moving solitons are elastic.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of pure-quartic solitons under parametric driving, opening possibilities for new soliton-based optical devices, but has no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Finite-State Gibbs Construction From A Recognition Cost
authors: Jonathan Washburn Megan Simons
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On a finite outcome space, the canonical Gibbs distribution is usually obtained by maximizing Shannon entropy at fixed mean of an externally supplied energy functional. This paper studies the finite-state consequences of a ratio-cost construction instead: after adopting the normalized d'Alembert degree-two closure called the Recognition Composition Law (RCL), with unit log-curvature calibration at the reference ratio, the continuous nontrivial positive branch is [MATH]. Given the induced cost vector [MATH], multinomial counting and convex duality recover the finite-state Gibbs weights and the identity [MATH]; the entropy-maximization steps are classical once the cost is fixed. New technical content includes a non-asymptotic Stirling bound and soft-shell constrained-type theorems for real-valued costs. A three-state example compares the Gibbs law to squared-log, affinity-as-energy, and Tsallis alternatives at the same cost vector and mean-cost constraint, with sample-size power calculations at fixed RCL ground truth. The framework is conditional on axioms (A1)--(A3) and restricted to finite outcome spaces with strictly positive weights; it does not derive the composition law from a more primitive principle.
tldr: This paper proposes a finite-state Gibbs distribution derived from a ratio-cost construction based on the Recognition Composition Law, rather than the standard energy functional, and compares it with alternative distributions.
motivation: To explore an alternative foundation for Gibbs distributions using a cost function derived from a composition law, potentially offering new insights into statistical mechanics or information theory.
method: The authors adopt the normalized d'Alembert degree-two closure (RCL) with unit log-curvature calibration, then use multinomial counting and convex duality to recover finite-state Gibbs weights. They also provide non-asymptotic Stirling bounds and soft-shell constrained-type theorems.
result: They derive the Gibbs weights and an identity relating cost and entropy, and compare the Gibbs law with squared-log, affinity-as-energy, and Tsallis alternatives in a three-state example, including sample-size power calculations.
conclusion: The framework is conditional on specific axioms and restricted to finite outcome spaces with positive weights; it does not derive the composition law from a more primitive principle, leaving room for future foundational work.

title: Spectral Separation Of Variables From Equivalent Lagrangian Systems
authors: Mattia Scomparin
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the dynamical equivalence of quadratic Lagrangians and its relation to separation of variables. We show that requiring two quadratic Lagrangians to generate the same Euler--Lagrange equations imposes a compatibility condition between the kinetic matrices and the potential. For constant symmetric kinetic matrices, this condition reduces to a commutation relation with the Hessian of the potential, yielding an orthogonal spectral decomposition of the configuration space. The equations of motion then decouple into independent subsystems: generically in block-separated form, and completely when the spectrum is simple. Applications include the Sawada--Kotera system and an [MATH]-dimensional extension of the H\'{e}non--Heiles model, where the classical integrable parameter regimes are recovered.
tldr: This paper studies the dynamical equivalence of quadratic Lagrangians and its relation to separation of variables in classical mechanics.
motivation: To understand when two quadratic Lagrangians yield the same Euler-Lagrange equations and how this leads to decoupled subsystems.
method: Derives compatibility conditions for kinetic matrices and potentials, reducing to commutation relations for constant symmetric matrices, leading to spectral decomposition.
result: The compatibility condition yields orthogonal spectral decomposition of configuration space, decoupling equations into independent subsystems; applied to Sawada-Kotera and Hénon-Heiles models.
conclusion: Provides a systematic method for identifying integrable regimes in classical systems, but has no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Spatiotemporal Decoupled Physics-informed Stone-Weierstrass Neural Operator For Long-time Prediction Of Time-dependent Parametric PDEs
authors: Shan Ding, Yongfu Tian, Lang Qin, Hongxiang Ma, Guofeng Su, Rui Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driven by rapid advances in artificial intelligence and modern GPU computing capabilities, deep learning methods based on the optimization paradigm have provided new pathways to solve spatiotemporal physical problems, whose mathematical core lies in solving partial differential equations (PDEs). As an emerging class of function-space learning methods, neural operators (NOs) have exhibited great potential in efficient PDE solving. However, existing mainstream neural operator frameworks suffer from critical bottlenecks when modeling time-dependent PDEs over long time horizons, including accuracy degradation, insufficient stability, high training costs, and excessive memory consumption, which severely limit their practical deployment. To address these challenges in long-time prediction with neural operators, we propose a novel spatiotemporally decoupled physics-informed neural operator architecture, termed the physics-informed Stone-Weierstrass neural operator (PI-SWNO). The design is theoretically grounded in the decoupling paradigm combining time-invariant spatial basis functions with time-varying evolution coefficients, as well as the Stone-Weierstrass approximation theorem. By encoding spatial and temporal information via two separate subnetworks, the framework structurally mitigates the accumulation of errors over extended time intervals. Furthermore, we introduce a time-marching batch-wise sampling strategy to resolve the memory bottleneck of full-range modeling over extended time spans, ensuring continuity and convergence of full-time-domain solutions.
tldr: Proposes a physics-informed neural operator (PI-SWNO) for long-time prediction of time-dependent parametric PDEs using spatiotemporal decoupling.
motivation: Existing neural operators suffer from accuracy degradation, instability, high training costs, and memory issues when modeling time-dependent PDEs over long time horizons.
method: Introduces a spatiotemporally decoupled architecture with separate subnetworks for spatial and temporal information, and a time-marching batch-wise sampling strategy to reduce memory usage.
result: The PI-SWNO framework mitigates error accumulation and memory bottlenecks, enabling stable long-time predictions.
conclusion: The approach offers a promising direction for efficient PDE solving, but its relevance to quantum information or thermodynamics is indirect.

title: Event-based Spatiotemporal Networks For Modelling Emergent Phenomena In Complex Systems
authors: Matthijs Romeijnders, Michiel van Boven, Francesco Corman, Carl D. Modes, Phillip Staniczencko, Debabrata Panja
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex systems display emergent phenomena that vary significantly across spatial and temporal scales. These variations originate from fine-grained system processes, yet arriving at macroscopic dynamics from micro-level data -- particularly when large, high-resolution datasets are available -- remains a persistent challenge. Here we develop event-based spatiotemporal networks, a computational modelling framework that encodes system processes as discrete events anchored in space and time. Event-based spatiotemporal networks offer a unified, flexible and efficient approach to generate emergent behaviour in complex systems across space and time from these events. We demonstrate the effectiveness of event-based spatiotemporal networks through two illustrative real-world applications. First, following a local outbreak of a novel respiratory pathogen in the Netherlands, spatiotemporal networks enable fine-grained tracking of transmission routes and infection patterns through space and time. Second, we use spatiotemporal networks to model propagation of delays in a public transportation system (S-bahn) around Z\"urich, Switzerland. We also discuss broader uses of event-based spatiotemporal networks in fields like developmental biology and community ecology, where focusing on events rather than static system states can improve data analysis, simulation, and collection strategies.
tldr: This paper introduces event-based spatiotemporal networks for modeling emergent phenomena in complex systems, with applications to epidemiology and transportation.
motivation: Complex systems exhibit emergent phenomena across scales, and deriving macroscopic dynamics from micro-level data remains challenging.
method: The authors develop a computational framework that encodes system processes as discrete events anchored in space and time, enabling efficient generation of emergent behavior.
result: The framework is demonstrated on two real-world applications: tracking a respiratory pathogen outbreak in the Netherlands and modeling delay propagation in a public transportation system in Zurich.
conclusion: Event-based spatiotemporal networks provide a unified, flexible approach for modeling complex systems, with potential applications in developmental biology and community ecology.

title: Fluorescence And Relaxation Dynamics Of Cesium In Argon Matrices: Multiple Trapping Sites And Host-Guest Interactions
authors: S. Lahs, H. Dinesan, S. Mahapatra, W. Chin, C. Crepin, L. Dontot, J. Douady, B. Gervais, D. Comparat
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the fluorescence and relaxation dynamics of Cs atoms embedded in a cryogenic argon matrix using spectroscopy measurements combined with diatomic-in-molecule (DIM) simulations. The data reveal complex emission spectra, large Stokes shifts, and slow relaxation effects, indicating strong host-guest interactions and substantial lattice reorganization. Although the spectra are superimposed on a broad background, possibly due to low-symmetry, defect-related, or grain-boundary trapping sites, the main spectral structure is consistent with two dominant trapping environments that give rise to two triplet absorption features with distinct fluorescence behavior of the doublet and singlet components. Polarization measurements further suggest that these sites may differ in symmetry, although a unique structural assignment remains difficult.
tldr: This paper studies fluorescence and relaxation dynamics of Cs atoms in argon matrices, focusing on host-guest interactions and trapping sites.
motivation: To understand the complex emission spectra and relaxation dynamics of Cs atoms embedded in cryogenic argon matrices, which are relevant for matrix isolation spectroscopy.
method: Spectroscopy measurements combined with diatomic-in-molecule (DIM) simulations.
result: Complex emission spectra with large Stokes shifts and slow relaxation, indicating strong host-guest interactions and lattice reorganization; two dominant trapping environments identified.
conclusion: The study provides insights into host-guest interactions in rare-gas matrices, but structural assignment remains difficult; further work needed for detailed understanding.

title: Reconstructing Temporal Multi-relational Firm Networks At Scale Using Large Language Models. The Case Of The Semiconductor Industry
authors: Seyda K\"ose, Christian Diem, Elma Dervic, Klaus Friesenbichler, Georg Heiler, Jan Hurt, Hernan Picatto, Peter Klimek
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The semiconductor industry is foundational to modern technology, yet its complex global multi-relational firm network remains poorly understood, posing challenges to scientists, firms, and policymakers. Traditional analysis relies on proprietary databases that are often expensive, incomplete, and slowly updated, limiting their ability to capture rapidly evolving dependencies. Here, we demonstrate that a novel, generalizable methodology combining Large Language Models (LLMs) with open web data can reconstruct this network and its structural dynamics at scale. We identify and classify supply-chain, partnership, and ownership links from 170 million semiconductor firm webpages, yielding a temporal network of over 1,300 linked firms. We validate link-extraction quality (Precision: 0.884; F1-score: 0.784), network overlap and complementarity with a proprietary database, and consistency with aggregate economic data. Our network reveals a temporary 9% decline in edges during the 2022 chip shortage, rapid increases in the centrality of AI supply-chain bottleneck firms such as NVIDIA, and geographic realignment of interfirm relations amid geopolitical turbulence. This generalizable framework overcomes barriers to transparency and provides essential, up-to-date maps for assessing resilience and informing policy across strategically relevant sectors.
tldr: This paper uses LLMs to reconstruct a temporal multi-relational firm network for the semiconductor industry from open web data.
motivation: To overcome the limitations of proprietary databases that are expensive, incomplete, and slow to update, and to provide a transparent, up-to-date map of the semiconductor industry network.
method: Combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with open web data to extract and classify supply-chain, partnership, and ownership links from 170 million semiconductor firm webpages, constructing a temporal network of over 1,300 firms.
result: Achieves high link-extraction quality (Precision 0.884, F1 0.784), reveals a 9% decline in edges during the 2022 chip shortage, increased centrality of AI supply-chain firms like NVIDIA, and geographic realignment of interfirm relations.
conclusion: The framework provides a generalizable method for reconstructing industry networks, enabling resilience assessment and policy-making in strategically relevant sectors.

title: Optimized Near-field Optical Response Via Adaptive Tip Illumination
authors: Tao Chen, Wei Wang, Ziyang Gan, Daniel Repp, Jinxin Zhan, Antony George, Henrik Schneidewind, Ulf Peschel, Andrey Turchanin, Volker Deckert
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of tip-enhanced optical microscopy is often limited by inefficient coupling of the excitation field to the plasmonic tip apex, as well as by thermal drift and optical aberrations. Here, we demonstrate that adaptive wavefront shaping based on Zernike mode provides a practical approach to achieving robust near-field optimisation at the tip apex. Using a sequential feedback algorithm, initially using the near-field signal, we narrow the illumination point-spread function and suppress sidelobes. This demonstrates that Zernike-mode control can be used for both aberration correction and field engineering. In tip-enhanced Raman measurements of a Janus MoSSe monolayer, conventional near-field optimisation increases the signal intensity by around 1.4 fold. A second optimisation step based directly on the Raman-band intensity yields a further 5 to 15 fold enhancement, depending on the specific tips used. These results establish a systematic, optics-based strategy for optimising tip fields, providing a transferable framework for improving tip-enhanced and related near-field spectroscopies.
tldr: This paper presents an adaptive wavefront shaping technique using Zernike modes to optimize the near-field optical response at a plasmonic tip apex for tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy.
motivation: Tip-enhanced optical microscopy suffers from inefficient coupling to the tip apex and issues like thermal drift and aberrations, limiting signal intensity.
method: The authors use a sequential feedback algorithm with Zernike-mode control to narrow the illumination point-spread function and suppress sidelobes, first optimizing the near-field signal and then the Raman-band intensity.
result: Conventional optimization increased signal by ~1.4-fold, and a second optimization based on Raman-band intensity yielded an additional 5- to 15-fold enhancement depending on the tip.
conclusion: This work establishes a systematic optics-based strategy for optimizing tip fields, providing a transferable framework for improving tip-enhanced and related near-field spectroscopies.

title: The Directed Abelian Sandpile Model On Cylinders
authors: Abdul Quadir, Nikita Kalinin, Ram Ramaswamy
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the abelian sandpile model in two dimensions on a directed cylindrical lattice with periodic transverse boundary conditions in the transverse direction and dissipation at one boundary. Recurrent configurations form a finite abelian group, and repeated grain addition at a specific site generates deterministic dynamics on this group. Using Dhar's formulation, the sandpile group is identified with the co-kernel of the reduced directed Laplacian. We show that the group structure admits an exact reduction to a transverse problem, allowing complete determination of its cyclic decomposition. Our results establish a direct connection between the algebraic structure of the sandpile group and the periodicity of the driven dynamics, establishing the manner in which the underlying algebraic structure governs both deterministic and stochastic evolution in directed sandpile.
tldr: This paper studies the algebraic structure and dynamics of the directed abelian sandpile model on a cylindrical lattice, focusing on its group decomposition and periodicity.
motivation: To understand the relationship between the algebraic structure of the sandpile group and the deterministic/stochastic dynamics in directed sandpile models.
method: Uses Dhar's formulation to identify the sandpile group with the co-kernel of the reduced directed Laplacian, and reduces the problem to a transverse one-dimensional problem to determine cyclic decomposition.
result: The group structure can be exactly reduced to a transverse problem, allowing complete determination of its cyclic decomposition, and establishing a direct connection between algebraic structure and periodicity of driven dynamics.
conclusion: The findings clarify how algebraic structure governs dynamics in directed sandpiles, but the paper is purely mathematical and not directly related to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Learning Selective Merge Policies For Deadline-Constrained Coded Caching Via Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Amirhossein Yousefiramandi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the coded caching, the server can use the information the users have cached to serve multiple users at a time by sending a single coded multi-casting message, i.e., the merged message, thereby relieving the peak network loads. However, for the delay-sensitive applications of the users, like the video streaming services, it becomes essential to choose which messages to merge online, considering the strict deadlines for each request. The problem, however, is that while the merge is helpful for the formation of the current coded multi-casting message, it can be harmful for the subsequent ones. We proposed a DRL-based solution that formulates the deadline-constrained coded delivery as a masked discrete-action queue-state control problem, while we trained a graph-attention policy network via proximal policy optimization. The policy network reduces the broadcast-packet expiration ratio [MATH] by [MATH] ([MATH] vs. [MATH]) with respect to the best coded multi-casting baseline (SACM++) on the uniform-demand benchmark, while also attaining the best broadcast-efficiency score [MATH] across the Track A battery among the coded multi-casting methods. The interesting fact we observed is that for the applications of the users with tight deadlines, the method of selective merging is better than the method of aggressive merging, i.e., the policy network learns to merge at only [MATH] rate, even though the same observation holds across the variations within the same simulator family.
tldr: This paper uses deep reinforcement learning to optimize coded caching delivery under deadline constraints, focusing on selective merging policies.
motivation: To address the challenge of merging messages in coded caching for delay-sensitive applications like video streaming, where merging decisions affect both current and future transmissions.
method: Formulates the problem as a masked discrete-action queue-state control problem and trains a graph-attention policy network using proximal policy optimization.
result: The DRL-based policy reduces broadcast-packet expiration ratio by a significant margin compared to the best baseline (SACM++) and achieves the best broadcast-efficiency score among coded multicasting methods.
conclusion: Selective merging is superior to aggressive merging under tight deadlines, and the learned policy adapts to different simulator variations.

title: Stochastic Compositional Optimization Via Hybrid Momentum Frank--Wolfe
authors: El Mahdi Chayti
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic compositional optimization minimizes objectives of the form [MATH], where [MATH] is accessible only through noisy stochastic queries. Existing methods for this problem assume that the outer function [MATH] is continuously differentiable, which excludes many practically important applications such as robust max-of-losses, Conditional Value-at-Risk, and norm regularizers. We propose the Hybrid Momentum Stochastic Frank--Wolfe algorithm, which drops the smoothness assumption on [MATH]. By combining a momentum-based Jacobian tracker with a Taylor-corrected function tracker, the algorithm feeds an entire stochastic linearization -- rather than a single gradient -- into a generalized linear minimization oracle. We establish an [MATH] convergence rate in the generalized Frank--Wolfe gap for non-convex objectives with [MATH]-Lipschitz outer functions, matching the optimal complexity for projection-free single-sample stochastic methods under expected smoothness. The analysis extends to heavy-tailed noise oracles with bounded [MATH]-th moments for [MATH] and recovers the deterministic rates of Vladarean et al (2023) as the noise vanishes.
tldr: This paper proposes a stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithm for compositional optimization without requiring smoothness of the outer function.
motivation: Existing methods for stochastic compositional optimization assume the outer function is continuously differentiable, which excludes many practical applications like robust max-of-losses and CVaR.
method: The Hybrid Momentum Stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithm combines a momentum-based Jacobian tracker with a Taylor-corrected function tracker to feed a stochastic linearization into a generalized linear minimization oracle.
result: The algorithm achieves an O(1/T) convergence rate in the generalized Frank-Wolfe gap for non-convex objectives with Lipschitz outer functions, matching optimal complexity for projection-free methods, and extends to heavy-tailed noise.
conclusion: The work provides a projection-free method for a broader class of compositional optimization problems, with theoretical guarantees that recover deterministic rates as noise vanishes.

title: Proposal-Guided Greedy Surrogate Refinement For PDE-Driven High-Dimensional Rare-Event Estimation
authors: George Karniadakis Zhiwei Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate surrogate construction for PDE-driven high-dimensional rare-event simulation is challenging when performance evaluations are expensive. Since a globally accurate surrogate may require many high-fidelity evaluations, adaptive importance sampling provides a natural localization tool: its evolving proposal distribution progressively identifies the failure-relevant region. Motivated by this observation, we propose a surrogate-assisted adaptive importance sampling framework that refines the surrogate locally along the evolving proposal, rather than over the entire input space. The surrogate combines an encoder with a neural network, providing a low-dimensional latent representation for both prediction and sample selection. At each adaptive iteration, candidates drawn from the current proposal are selected by a greedy latent-space rule balancing proximity to the estimated failure boundary and sample diversity. The selected samples are evaluated by the high-fidelity model and used to refine the surrogate, which then guides the subsequent cross-entropy-type adaptive proposal update. We establish one-step proposal stability bounds under local surrogate errors, together with surrogate-induced misclassification and finite-sample estimation error bounds. Numerical experiments on multimodal benchmarks and PDE-driven rare-event problems up to 100 dimensions show that the proposed method achieves accuracy comparable to true-model adaptive importance sampling while requiring substantially fewer high-fidelity evaluations.
tldr: A surrogate-assisted adaptive importance sampling framework for high-dimensional rare-event estimation in PDE-driven problems.
motivation: Accurate surrogate construction for rare-event simulation is challenging when high-fidelity evaluations are expensive; globally accurate surrogates are inefficient.
method: Proposes a greedy latent-space sample selection rule to refine a neural-network-based surrogate locally along the evolving proposal distribution of adaptive importance sampling.
result: Achieves accuracy comparable to true-model adaptive importance sampling with substantially fewer high-fidelity evaluations on benchmarks and PDE problems up to 100 dimensions.
conclusion: The method reduces computational cost for rare-event estimation; future work may extend to broader classes of PDEs and uncertainty quantification.

title: Implicit Dynamical Tensor Train Approximation For Kinetic Equations With Stiff Fokker--Planck Collisions
authors: Jingwei Hu Geshuo Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-rank methods for kinetic equations have attracted increasing attention due to their effectiveness in reducing the high dimensionality of phase space. In our previous work [G. Wang & J. Hu, J. Comput. Phys. 558 (2026) 114884], we developed a dynamical low-rank method based on the projector-splitting integrator in tensor-train (TT) format, in which explicit time integration is employed in all substeps. As a result, the method is subject to severe stability constraints in the strongly collisional regimes. In this paper, we consider kinetic equations with the (nonlinear) Fokker--Planck collision operator and develop a dynamical low-rank method that employs implicit or implicit-explicit (IMEX) discretizations in appropriate substeps to overcome stiffness. In these implicit substeps, the resulting equations can be formulated as matrix or tensor Sylvester equations, for which we propose efficient direct solvers by exploiting their underlying structure. The overall computational cost of the proposed method scales linearly with respect to the number of grid points in a single velocity dimension, comparable to that of a fully explicit low-rank scheme. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method on several representative kinetic test problems.
tldr: This paper develops an implicit dynamical low-rank method for kinetic equations with stiff Fokker-Planck collisions, focusing on computational efficiency for high-dimensional phase space.
motivation: Explicit low-rank methods for kinetic equations suffer from severe stability constraints in strongly collisional regimes. The authors aim to overcome stiffness while maintaining linear computational cost.
method: They propose a dynamical low-rank approximation in tensor-train format with implicit or IMEX discretizations in appropriate substeps, solving resulting matrix/tensor Sylvester equations with efficient direct solvers.
result: The method achieves linear scaling with respect to grid points in a single velocity dimension, comparable to explicit schemes, and demonstrates accuracy and efficiency on several kinetic test problems.
conclusion: The work provides a stable and efficient low-rank solver for kinetic equations with Fokker-Planck collisions, with potential extensions to other collisional operators and higher dimensions.

title: Control Of The Fluidic Pinball Using The Quadratic-Quadratic Regulator
authors: Jeff Borggaard Ali Bouland
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fluidic pinball presents a significant benchmark for nonlinear flow control, managing the complex interactions of three cylinder wakes. This study addresses the stabilization of the fluidic pinball to its unstable steady-state solution using a model-based nonlinear feedback strategy. We propose a framework that combines interpolatory model order reduction (IMOR) with the quadratic-quadratic regulator (QQR), a feedback control methodology that is specifically suited to the quadratic nonlinearity of the Navier-Stokes equations. A finite element model (FEM) of the problem coupled with IMOR is used to produce a reduced-order model (ROM) that accurately represents the input-output dynamics of the actuated wake. The performance of the QQR control is evaluated against the traditional linear feedback control for two different Reynolds numbers, [MATH] and [MATH]. At [MATH], the QQR controller is able to stabilize the wake and reaches the desired performance criteria 40.1\% faster than using a linear feedback controller. More significantly, at [MATH], the QQR controller successfully stabilizes the wake, whereas the linear controller fails to overcome the nonlinearity of the flow. The QQR control effectively suppresses vortex shedding, resulting in the elimination of lift oscillations and a reduction in the drag coefficient. These results demonstrate that the IMOR-QQR framework provides an effective model-based control strategy that can manage nonlinear hydrodynamic instabilities in such complex wake flows.
tldr: This paper applies a nonlinear control strategy (QQR) to stabilize the fluidic pinball flow, demonstrating improved performance over linear control.
motivation: To address the challenge of stabilizing nonlinear wake flows, which is important for flow control applications.
method: Combines interpolatory model order reduction (IMOR) with the quadratic-quadratic regulator (QQR) to design a feedback controller for the Navier-Stokes equations.
result: At Re=100, QQR stabilizes the wake 40.1% faster than linear control; at Re=200, QQR succeeds while linear control fails.
conclusion: The IMOR-QQR framework is effective for controlling nonlinear hydrodynamic instabilities, with potential for broader flow control applications.

title: PrismQuant: Rate-Distortion-Optimal Vector Quantization For Gaussian-Mixture Sources
authors: Bumsu Park, Chanho Park, Youngmok Park, Namyoon Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a Gaussian source under mean-squared error (MSE), classical transform coding is rate--distortion (RD) optimal: the Karhunen--Loeve transform (KLT) diagonalizes the covariance, reverse waterfilling allocates the bits, and scalar quantization closes the loop. This elegant story breaks down for multimodal sources, where no single covariance can capture heterogeneous local geometries, and the RD function loses its closed form. We revisit this problem through Gaussian-mixture sources and develop a constructive RD theory for them. Our key finding is that the mixture structure incurs only a component label cost. Conditioned on the active mixture component, each branch is Gaussian; the challenge is allocating bits across heterogeneous branches. We prove that the genie-aided conditional RD function is governed by a single global reverse-waterfilling level shared across all components and eigenmodes. Building on this result, we introduce PrismQuant, which transmits the component label losslessly and encodes the residual using the component-matched KLT, followed by scalar quantization, achieving a rate of H(C)/n bits per source dimension of the converse, with a vanishing asymptotic gap. We further develop a practical implementation based on EM-driven Gaussian-mixture learning, component-adaptive KLTs, and entropy-constrained scalar quantization (ECSQ). Experiments on synthetic Gaussian mixtures show that PrismQuant closely approaches the theoretical RD bound, while experiments on real-world channel-state-information (CSI) data demonstrate competitive or superior performance compared with transformer-based learned codecs at more than one order of magnitude smaller model size.
tldr: PrismQuant proposes a rate-distortion-optimal vector quantization scheme for Gaussian-mixture sources, achieving near-optimal compression by combining component label transmission with component-matched KLT and entropy-constrained scalar quantization.
motivation: Classical transform coding fails for multimodal sources because a single covariance cannot capture heterogeneous local geometries, and the rate-distortion function loses its closed form.
method: The authors prove that the genie-aided conditional RD function for Gaussian mixtures is governed by a single global reverse-waterfilling level across all components and eigenmodes. They then develop PrismQuant, which transmits the component label losslessly and encodes the residual using component-matched KLT followed by entropy-constrained scalar quantization.
result: PrismQuant achieves a rate of H(C)/n bits per source dimension with a vanishing asymptotic gap to the theoretical bound. Experiments on synthetic mixtures and real-world CSI data show it closely approaches the RD bound and outperforms transformer-based codecs with much smaller model size.
conclusion: The work provides a constructive RD theory for Gaussian mixtures and a practical codec that is both theoretically optimal and computationally efficient, with potential applications in compression of multimodal data.

title: Auto-Conditioned Frank-Wolfe Algorithms
authors: Khanh-Hung Giang-Tran, Soroosh Shafiee, Nam Ho-Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2605.15512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frank-Wolfe methods are projection-free algorithms for constrained optimization whose practical performance often depends critically on the choice of step size. Classical closed-loop step-size rules typically require prior knowledge of a global smoothness constant, while line-search variants avoid this requirement at the cost of additional function evaluations and implementation overhead. In this paper, we develop a fully auto-conditioned framework for Frank-Wolfe-type methods. The framework replaces the global Lipschitz constant in closed-loop step sizes with a local Lipschitz estimator computed from first-order information along the iterates. We show that this abstraction captures several important projection-free subroutines, including standard Frank-Wolfe, Matching Pursuit, pairwise Frank-Wolfe, and away-step Frank-Wolfe. For the resulting general class of methods, we establish convergence to stationary points in the nonconvex setting and recover the standard sublinear convergence guarantees in the convex setting, without requiring prior knowledge of a global smoothness constant. We further show that, when specialized to particular Frank-Wolfe variants and combined with additional structural assumptions, the same auto-conditioned framework yields accelerated convergence rates. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed methods provide substantial practical improvements over line-search-based alternatives, highlighting the benefits of adapting to local curvature while retaining the simplicity of closed-loop step-size rules.
tldr: This paper develops an auto-conditioned framework for Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithms that adaptively estimates local Lipschitz constants, eliminating the need for global smoothness knowledge.
motivation: Classical Frank-Wolfe methods require prior knowledge of a global smoothness constant or rely on line-search, which adds computational overhead. The authors aim to create a fully adaptive step-size rule that is both efficient and theoretically sound.
method: The framework replaces the global Lipschitz constant with a local Lipschitz estimator computed from first-order information along iterates.
